strengths: Integrates temporal self-attention with a frequency-domain attention module that is conditioned on time granularity, which is a reasonable direction for multivariate time-series foundation models.
Adapts autoregressive blank infilling from NLP to time-series pretraining, aiming for a generative task-agnostic framework without task-specific architectural changes.
Evaluates the model on three generative tasks (forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection) and includes some ablation studies and pretraining comparisons.
Uses large-scale UTSD-12G pretraining and reports competitive results on several downstream datasets.
The low-rank Fourier knowledge attention design is technically plausible and could be efficient if properly specified and validated.
The appendix provides some additional dataset statistics, implementation details, and visualizations.
weaknesses: The central claim that GTM outperforms SOTA methods across all generative tasks is not supported by the reported tables. For example, PatchTST beats GTM on weather 336 forecasting and Electricity imputation, TTME beats GTM on several forecasting settings, DLinear beats GTM on MSL anomaly detection, and TimesNet beats GTM on PSM anomaly detection.

Key recent time-series foundation model baselines are missing, including TimesFM, MOIRAI, Timer, Lag-Llama, and others, despite the paper positioning GTM as a general MTS foundation model. Many reported baseline numbers are cited rather than reproduced under a unified protocol, making comparisons unreliable.

The empirical finding about time granularity is largely intuitive and potentially confounded: different sampling rates and domains naturally induce different frequency-domain distributions. The analysis lacks normalization by Nyquist frequency, resampling controls, statistical tests, or evidence that granularity rather than domain/dataset identity causes the observed differences.

The paper repeatedly claims to investigate universal knowledge representation from first principles, but never formally defines universal knowledge or universal representation, and the evaluation only covers three generative tasks rather than the broader task space implied by the claims.

The method description is insufficient for reproducibility. In particular, Eq. 3 has dimensional inconsistencies (e.g., A_i in R^{385x1}, B_i in R^{1x385}, while the feature dimension is stated as 768), the granularity quintuple construction is unclear, and it is ambiguous whether forecasting uses zero-shot evaluation or fine-tuned weights.

Novelty is limited. Combining temporal and frequency-domain modeling is well studied in prior work such as FEDformer, Fredformer, FITS, and TimeMixer++, while autoregressive blank infilling is adapted from GLM. The specific low-rank granularity-conditioned attention is incremental, and 'first' claims are overstated.

Evaluation protocols are inconsistent and potentially unfair: baselines are trained/fine-tuned under different settings, some are cited from prior papers with different splits or preprocessing, and the paper explicitly notes the lack of a unified benchmark in its limitations section.

Ablations are narrow. They only remove frequency/granularity modules, but do not ablate the pretraining strategy, rank size, number of granularity modules, global frequency module, positional encodings, or the low-rank vs. full-rank design. There is also no analysis of the learned granularity attention weights.

Pretraining gains are modest and sometimes negligible (e.g., 0.5% on traffic/electricity forecasting and 0.5% on Electricity imputation MAE), with no statistical significance tests, parameter counts, or computational cost analysis to justify the foundation-model claim.

Potential data leakage is not convincingly ruled out. UTSD-12G may overlap with downstream datasets such as ETT, Weather, Electricity, or Traffic; the paper asserts no leakage but does not provide a detailed overlap analysis or dataset exclusion list.

The writing and presentation contain many typographical and notational issues (e.g., 'devided', 'cript', 'Poj', inconsistent equations and table formatting), and some claims in the text conflict with the tables and experimental descriptions.

The time-granularity mechanism relies on calendar components (day/hour/minute/second/millisecond), which may not capture irregular, event-driven, or non-calendar periodicities common in general time series, limiting the claimed universality.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: building multivariate time-series foundation models that can adapt across multiple generative downstream tasks.

The proposed GTM combines several relevant ideas, including patching, channel independence, time/frequency-domain processing, time-granularity conditioning, and GLM-style blank infilling pre-training.
The empirical evaluation spans forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection across multiple datasets, and includes some ablations and pre-training comparisons.
Some individual results, especially on certain forecasting/imputation/anomaly datasets, suggest that the combined design can be competitive.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim that different time granularities exhibit distinct frequency-domain joint distributions is largely expected and trivial: changing the sampling rate changes the frequency axis and resolution, so the plotted distributions naturally differ. The paper provides no rigorous statistical test or controlled analysis showing this is a meaningful new inductive bias rather than a consequence of different units/scales.

Novelty is overstated. Fourier/frequency attention, low-rank frequency modules, time-granularity conditioning, and autoregressive blank infilling are all heavily related to existing work (e.g., FEDformer, Fredformer, FITS, GLM, MoE-style gating). The claim of being the first to integrate Fourier knowledge attention in an MTS foundation model is not convincingly supported.

The paper claims a general/universal foundation model, but only generative tasks are evaluated. Classification is listed as out of scope in Table 1, and there is no zero-shot or cross-domain transfer evaluation to unseen granularities/domains. The model still appears to require downstream fine-tuning, making the 'without adaptation' claim ambiguous and overstated.

The Fourier knowledge attention formulation is unclear and appears to be a softmax-gated mixture of low-rank linear transforms in the frequency domain rather than a genuine attention mechanism. The time-granularity encoding is also poorly defined: the quintuple [day,hour,minute,second,ms] representation is inconsistent with the 4-second, 5-minute, 1-hour, and 1-day examples, and it is unclear how irregular or unseen granularities would be handled.

The experimental results contain serious inconsistencies. For example, Table 3 and Table 13 give contradictory Informer imputation numbers for Weather/Electricity, Table 4 and Table 8 report different GTM anomaly-detection averages, and Table 6 contains a duplicated electricity row. Such inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported results.

The SOTA claims are not supported by the tables. GTM is not best on all forecasting datasets (e.g., TTME is better on some ETTh1/Electricity settings), is worse than PatchTST on Electricity imputation, and is not best on several anomaly-detection datasets (e.g., DLinear on MSL, GPT4TS on SMD, UP2ME/TimesNet/FEDformer on PSM). The textual claims overstate the empirical evidence.

The evaluation lacks important baselines and controls. For forecasting, recent foundation models such as Timer, TimesFM, MOIRAI, and Lag-Llama are not compared; for anomaly detection, specialized methods such as Anomaly Transformer, DCdetector, and MEMTO are missing; for imputation, SAITS is missing. The selective baseline exclusion is not convincingly justified.

Reproducibility is weak. No code or model release is mentioned, key training details are incomplete (parameter count, compute, random seeds, threshold selection for anomaly detection), and there is no verification that UTSD-12G pre-training data does not overlap with downstream datasets. The imputation protocol also removes patching even though pre-training is patch-based, and this adaptation is not explained.

Ablations are limited and show only small gains. The contribution of the proposed Fourier knowledge attention and time-granularity modules is modest on several datasets, and there is no ablation of the blank-infilling pre-training strategy against alternative pre-training objectives, masking strategies, or output projection designs.

The paper is difficult to verify due to numerous typographical, notation, and formatting errors (e.g., 'devided', 'cript', 'LinPoj', 'Phae-Frequency', 'pred_len', inconsistent table columns). The writing and presentation do not meet the standard expected for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: universal knowledge representation for multivariate time-series foundation models.
Proposes a multi-task model that combines temporal and frequency-domain information with time-granularity-aware attention, a relatively novel combination for MTS foundation models.
Adapts autoregressive blank infilling from NLP to MTS pretraining, enabling a single model to be applied to multiple generative tasks without task-specific heads.
Reports experiments on forecasting, imputation, and anomaly detection, with some strong results and ablation studies supporting the frequency/granularity components.
Includes a large-scale pretraining setup on UTSD-12G and demonstrates gains from pretraining over training from scratch.
weaknesses: The central empirical finding—that different time granularities have different frequency-domain distributions—is largely expected and not analyzed deeply enough to justify the claimed importance for universal representation.

The Fourier knowledge attention mechanism is mathematically unclear and potentially inconsistent: dimensions of H_Fft, A_i, B_i, and the stated feature dimension (768 vs. 385) do not align, and the low-rank matrices are described with confusing shapes; Eq. 3 omits key definitions and derivations.

The pretraining framework is an incremental adaptation of GLM-style blank infilling; the paper does not compare against alternative pretraining strategies (masked, autoregressive, contrastive) and the claim of being the first in time-series analysis is not convincingly established.

Evaluation is incomplete and not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier claim of SOTA across all generative tasks: many recent MTS foundation models (e.g., TimesFM, MOIRAI, Timer, Lag-Llama) are not compared, several baselines use cited numbers under different settings, and the paper admits a lack of unified benchmarks.

The claim of outperforming SOTA across all generative tasks is overstated: GTM is not best on several settings, e.g., imputation on Electricity is third behind PatchTST and GPT4TS, and anomaly detection on MSL/SMD/PSM is beaten by other baselines.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release is mentioned, and key implementation details are missing, such as how different forecasting horizons and imputation lengths are generated from the same output projection, how the time-granularity query is constructed, and how task-specific preprocessing is applied.

Ablation studies are limited: they only remove frequency attention and time-granularity modules, but do not ablate the pretraining strategy, masking design, output projection, instance normalization, patching, or channel independence.

Clarity and writing quality need substantial improvement: numerous typos and notation errors (e.g., 'GPT4T5', 'devided', 'P_cript', 'Phae', 'LinPoj'), duplicated rows (Electricity/electricity), and inconsistent table labels make the paper harder to trust and reproduce.

Positioning is somewhat inconsistent: the model is presented as a unified foundation model, but it does not support classification tasks, and the abstract/introduction overclaim compared with the reported experimental scope.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: building a general time-series foundation model that can adapt to multiple generative tasks without task-specific architecture changes.
Introduces a novel frequency-domain attention module that incorporates time-granularity-aware keys, a relatively underexplored dimension in time-series representation learning.

Proposes a hybrid masking pre-training strategy that unifies masked reconstruction and autoregressive generation, together with 2D positional encoding and span shuffling, which is conceptually appealing for multi-task time-series modeling.
Conducts extensive experiments spanning long-term forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, classification, zero-shot and few-shot settings, ablations, scalability, and efficiency analysis.
Reports strong empirical results on several benchmarks and often achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance, especially on average across datasets.
Provides detailed implementation settings, dataset statistics, pseudo-code, and error-bar analysis for some experiments, aiding reproducibility to some extent.
Includes model efficiency and scaling analyses, which are valuable for practical deployment of time-series foundation models.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated. The paper claims GTM consistently outperforms SOTA, but GTM is not best in many individual settings: e.g., TTME has lower average MSE on ETTh1 in Table 1; Time-MOE-Base is better on all ETTh1 prediction lengths and several ETTm1 settings in Table 20; PatchTST is better on Electricity imputation; DLinear is better on MSL anomaly detection; UP2ME, GPT4TS, TimesNet, and FEDformer are better on PSM anomaly detection; GPT4TS/TimesNet are much better on Japanese Vowels classification.

The core pre-training framework is insufficiently ablated. The paper claims hybrid masking, 2D positional encoding, and span shuffling as main contributions, but the ablation study only examines the frequency module and time-granularity-aware module. There is no ablation isolating the benefits of hybrid masking, pred_ratio, span shuffling, or 2D positional encoding, so the central pre-training contribution is not well supported.

Potential data leakage is not adequately addressed. The model is pre-trained on UTSD-12G, which likely contains or overlaps with domains/datasets commonly used for downstream evaluation such as ETT, Weather, Electricity, and Traffic. The manuscript claims no downstream task-related data is included, but provides no explicit overlap analysis, exclusion lists, or dataset-level provenance to substantiate this. This threatens the validity of the zero-shot and fine-tuning results.

Evaluation comparisons are not fully rigorous. Many forecasting baseline results are cited from prior papers rather than reproduced under the same experimental protocol, look-back windows, and preprocessing. The paper also excludes TSFMs that require pre-training and fine-tuning on downstream datasets, which removes important and standard baselines. Error bars are reported only for GTM, not for baselines, so statistical significance of improvements is unclear.

The method description is sometimes unclear. The Fourier attention equations do not clearly explain the shape and role of the low-rank matrices and how they act on the frequency-transformed representations. The combination of full attention for reconstruction and causal attention for autoregressive generation is asserted but not detailed. The 2D positional encoding and span shuffling are also under-specified.

The reproducibility statement is incomplete: the manuscript says code and implementation details are available at a URL, but the URL is missing. Some tasks use different preprocessing (e.g., omitting patching for imputation), which slightly weakens the claim of seamless task-agnostic adaptation.
The scalability analysis is limited to a few datasets (mainly ETTh1 and Weather), which is not sufficient to establish broad scaling behavior for time-series foundation models.

The positioning of GTM as the first generative-task-agnostic TSFM may be too strong. Related multi-task TSFMs such as UniTS, TIMER, and UP2ME already support multiple generative tasks, and the distinction between “task-agnostic” and “requiring only a projection-head change” should be argued more carefully.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: building general-purpose time-series foundation models that can transfer across generative and discriminative tasks.
Combines several sensible ingredients: frequency-domain modeling, time-granularity conditioning, hybrid masked/autoregressive pre-training, and 2D positional encoding.
The experimental scope is broad, covering forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, classification, zero-/few-shot evaluation, ablations, scaling, and efficiency analysis.
Appendices provide additional results, error bars for forecasting, and some implementation details, which is useful for reproducibility if further clarified.
Some reported results are competitive on several datasets, suggesting the overall framework may have practical potential after substantial revision.
weaknesses: Major technical concern: the Fourier attention appears to apply FFT over the embedding dimension rather than the temporal/patch sequence. The low-rank matrices are specified as A in R^{385x1}, B in R^{1x385}, and with D=768, 385 is exactly the rfft size. This means the module is likely performing frequency transforms over hidden feature channels, not over time-series time steps. As written, the central claim that it captures time-granularity-aware temporal frequency patterns is unsupported and conceptually mismatched with Figure 1.

The paper overclaims novelty and generality. It claims to be the first generative-task-agnostic TSFM, but adaptation still requires task-specific changes such as removing masking, omitting patching, replacing the projection head, using reconstruction thresholds for anomaly detection, and task-specific preprocessing. This contradicts the task-agnostic positioning and weakens the claimed contribution.

Evaluation is not sufficiently fair or controlled. Main tables mix cited numbers from different protocols, look-back windows, data splits, and fine-tuning settings. Several claims of consistent SOTA are contradicted by the results: TTM_E beats GTM on ETTh1 MSE in Table 1, Time-MOE-Base beats GTM on several ETTh1 forecasting metrics in Table 20, and TimesFM substantially beats GTM on ETTm1 zero-shot MSE in Table 5.

Baseline averages are biased by missing entries. In Tables 1 and 5, several baselines lack results on some datasets, yet averages are compared directly. Selective reporting makes aggregate claims unreliable.

Ablations do not validate the main pre-training contributions. There is no systematic ablation of hybrid masking, random vs. tail masking, span shuffling, 2D positional encoding, or the unified reconstruction/autoregressive objective. Only frequency/granularity modules are ablated.

Statistical significance is weak. Many improvements are tiny and within the reported error bars, and because baselines are not re-run under the same conditions, the gains cannot be attributed to GTM with confidence. Error bars are also limited mainly to forecasting.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The code/implementation link is blank, and several critical details are missing: FFT axis, handling of complex values, attention masking for full vs. causal attention, classification aggregation, span-shuffling procedure, and exact granularity encodings for all datasets.

Potential data leakage/contamination is not addressed. The UTSD-12G pre-training corpus includes Energy, Environment, and Transport domains, while downstream benchmarks include ETTh/ETTm, Weather, Electricity, and Traffic. The claim that no downstream task-related data is included is not verified.

Classification evaluation is weak. The comparison uses mainly TSFM baselines rather than strong specialized time-series classification methods, and GTM is not clearly better on several datasets, e.g., Japanese Vowels, SelfRegulationSCP1, PEMS-SF.

Anomaly detection claims are overstated. GTM is not uniformly best: DLinear is better on MSL, GPT4TS is better on SMD, and UP2ME is much better on PSM in Table 3. The statement that GTM achieves the highest F1 across all baselines is false.
Scalability analysis is superficial. It shows monotonic improvement curves but does not fit scaling laws or test enough model sizes, tasks, and data scales to support strong scaling-law claims.

Clarity and presentation need substantial improvement. There are typos, inconsistent terminology, unclear equations, contradictory descriptions of task-specific adaptation, and incomplete figure/table formatting.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: building a general time-series foundation model that can serve multiple generative and discriminative tasks.
The frequency-domain attention and time-granularity-aware design are well motivated by empirical FFT/KDE analyses in Figure 1, which is a useful observation for the time-series community.

The proposed hybrid pre-training strategy combines reconstruction and autoregressive objectives via random masking, controlled tail masking, 2D positional encoding, and span shuffling; this is a plausible recipe for unified representation learning.
The empirical study is broad, covering forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection, classification, zero/few-shot transfer, ablation, scalability, and efficiency analyses.
The ablation and scaling studies provide some evidence that the Fourier attention and larger pre-training data/model sizes contribute to performance.
The paper is generally well organized and the results are presented across a wide range of tasks and datasets.
weaknesses: The central claim that GTM consistently outperforms SOTA is not supported by the reported results. GTM loses or ties on several metrics, e.g., ETTh1, Weather, Traffic, Electricity in forecasting; Electricity in imputation; MSL and PSM in anomaly detection; and Japanese Vowels, Heartbeat, EthanolConcentration, PEMS-SF in classification. Appendix results also show Time-MOE-Base and Sundial-Small outperforming GTM in several settings.

The evaluation protocol is not sufficiently unified or fair. Many forecasting baselines are cited from prior papers instead of being reproduced under the same pre-training/fine-tuning setup, some baselines lack MAE or certain datasets, and the strongest recent TSFMs are mostly relegated to the appendix. This weakens claims of state-of-the-art performance.

Novelty is incremental. Frequency-domain attention, low-rank spectral modules, and hybrid masked/autoregressive pre-training are related to prior work such as FEDformer, GLM-style blank infilling, and existing TSFM pre-training strategies. The time-granularity-aware component is the main new idea, but its novelty and advantage are not deeply analyzed.

Technical details of the Fourier attention module are unclear or inconsistent. For example, the low-rank matrices are stated as A in R^{385x1} and B in R^{1x385}, but it is not clear how these dimensions match H_FFT, what the query q is in q_f = q W_f^Q, how the five granularity keys are chosen, and how exactly full vs. causal attention is combined during pre-training.

The paper overclaims task-agnostic adaptation. GTM still requires task-specific handling such as removing masking, omitting patching for imputation, changing the projection head for classification, applying anomaly thresholds, and fine-tuning for downstream tasks. This contradicts the strong 'without any task-specific modifications' framing.

Reproducibility is limited: the code link is blank in the manuscript, several implementation details are deferred to an appendix or omitted, and the large-scale pre-training setup may be difficult to reproduce without significant compute resources.

The ablation study focuses mainly on forecasting and does not isolate the contributions of the hybrid masking strategy, span shuffling, 2D positional encoding, or different Fourier attention variants. It is therefore unclear which components are truly essential.

Efficiency claims are mixed: GTM has higher training memory and slower inference than some baselines such as Time-MOE and GPT-2 in Table 9, so the claim of strong industrial efficiency is not uniformly supported.

Some experimental improvements are small and may not be statistically significant, while error-bar analysis is largely deferred to the appendix and not provided for all tasks. This makes it difficult to judge the robustness of the main conclusions.
